notes.front: What does ‘weight and balance’ mean for a small UA?
notes.back: The aircraft’s total weight and how that weight is distributed, both of which must stay within the manufacturer’s limits.
notes.explanation: Before any flight the remote PIC should check the aircraft is correctly loaded; compliance with the limits is critical to flight safety.
notes.example: Fitting a heavier camera and a spotlight: check the total against the maximum weight and that the load sits where the maker allows.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.2.1, p. B-1

notes.front: What is the center of gravity (CG)?
notes.back: The point at which all of the aircraft’s weight may be considered concentrated; supported there, it would balance in any attitude.
notes.explanation: Its position has a great bearing on stability, so makers set limits for where it may be.
notes.example: Hanging a payload off one side of a quadcopter moves the CG towards that side.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Weight”, p. 29

notes.front: What is a stall?
notes.back: A sudden loss of lift when the air meeting a wing at too steep an angle can no longer flow smoothly over it.
notes.explanation: Any aircraft can be stalled at any airspeed if that angle becomes too great, for example in a steep turn.
notes.example: A fixed-wing drone pulled into a very tight turn close to the ground can stall and drop.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Load Factors and Stalling Speeds”, p. 31

notes.front: What is load factor?
notes.back: The ratio of the lift being produced to the aircraft’s weight, measured in Gs: the load its structure carries in a maneuver.
notes.explanation: Any force that bends the flight path, such as a turn or pull-up, adds stress; too much can overload the structure.
notes.example: A load factor of 3 means the structure carries three times the aircraft’s weight: 3 Gs.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Load Factors”, p. 30

notes.front: What is an aircraft’s stability?
notes.back: Its built-in tendency to correct for disturbances and return to, or continue on, its original flight path.
notes.explanation: It is mainly a design characteristic, and it affects how easily the aircraft can be maneuvered and controlled.
notes.example: After a gust tips it, a stable aircraft settles back to level flight on its own.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Stability”, p. 30

notes.front: What is maneuverability?
notes.back: The quality that lets an aircraft be maneuvered easily and withstand the stresses of maneuvers.
notes.explanation: It depends on weight, inertia, size and location of controls, structural strength and power, and is a design characteristic.
notes.example: A light racing drone turns sharply; a heavy lift drone turns slowly.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Stability”, p. 30

notes.front: What is controllability?
notes.back: The aircraft’s ability to respond to the pilot’s control inputs, especially in flight path and attitude.
notes.explanation: It describes the response to control, regardless of how stable the aircraft is.
notes.example: A drone that answers the sticks crisply is highly controllable.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Stability”, p. 30

notes.front: What is performance data for a small UA?
notes.back: The manufacturer’s figures for how the aircraft performs, such as takeoff, climb, range, endurance, descent and landing.
notes.explanation: Using it is essential to fly within the aircraft’s capabilities and limitations.
notes.example: A manual stating 30 minutes’ endurance with no payload, and less with a camera fitted.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.1, p. B-1

notes.front: Whose weight and balance limits must the remote PIC follow?
notes.back: The manufacturer’s or builder’s limits. Follow them closely.
notes.explanation: Compliance with them is critical to flight safety, and an overweight aircraft may become unsafe.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.2.1, p. B-1

notes.front: Is it always safe to take off at the maximum gross takeoff weight (the heaviest the maker allows at launch)?
notes.back: No. High density altitude, from high elevation, high temperature or high humidity, may require a lower weight.
notes.explanation: The maximum weight is a limit, not a guarantee that the aircraft can lift it in all conditions.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.2.1.1, p. B-1

notes.front: Besides density altitude, which launch-site factors may require reducing weight before flight?
notes.back: The launch area’s length, surface and slope; the surface wind; and nearby obstacles.
notes.explanation: Each affects takeoff and climb performance.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.2.1.1, p. B-1

notes.front: How can a small UA’s weight change during flight?
notes.back: By using up or dropping something it carries, such as releasing a package (a “jettisonable load”).
notes.explanation: Any in-flight weight change directly affects performance. For manned aircraft, fuel burn is the most common weight change.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.2.1.2, p. B-1

notes.front: As an aircraft gets lighter in flight, what improves and what may get worse?
notes.back: Performance improves, but balance may get worse.
notes.explanation: Removing weight from one place can move the CG.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.2.1.2, p. B-1

notes.front: Is the CG a fixed point on the aircraft?
notes.back: No. It depends on how the weight is distributed, and shifts when loads are moved or used up.
notes.explanation: The remote PIC should work out how the CG will shift and what that will do.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.2.2, p. B-1

notes.front: What does operating with the CG outside its approved limits cause?
notes.back: Control difficulty.
notes.explanation: Adverse balance affects flight characteristics much like excess weight does.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Weight and Balance”, p. 32

notes.front: What must you do if the CG is outside allowable limits after loading, or will not stay within them in flight?
notes.back: Relocate or shed weight before flight.
notes.explanation: Flight should not be attempted until the CG is within limits.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.2.2, p. B-2

notes.front: What does operating above the maximum weight limit do?
notes.back: It compromises the aircraft’s structural integrity and harms its performance.
notes.explanation: If weight exceeds the lift the aircraft can generate, it may be incapable of flight.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Weight and Balance”, p. 32

notes.front: Where does poor performance from improper loading usually first show?
notes.back: During takeoff.
notes.explanation: An overloaded aircraft may not leave the ground, or may fly with unexpectedly poor characteristics.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Effects of Weight”, p. 33

notes.front: How does overloading affect takeoff performance?
notes.back: A higher takeoff speed and a longer takeoff run.
notes.explanation: Excessive weight reduces performance in almost every respect; these are among the most important deficiencies.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Effects of Weight”, p. 33

notes.front: How does overloading affect climb performance?
notes.back: A reduced rate and angle of climb, and a lower maximum altitude.
notes.explanation: Excessive weight reduces performance in almost every respect; these are among the most important deficiencies.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Effects of Weight”, p. 33

notes.front: How does overloading affect cruise performance?
notes.back: A shorter range and a reduced cruising speed.
notes.explanation: Excessive weight reduces performance in almost every respect; these are among the most important deficiencies.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Effects of Weight”, p. 33

notes.front: How does overloading affect handling performance?
notes.back: Reduced maneuverability and a higher stalling speed.
notes.explanation: Excessive weight reduces performance in almost every respect; these are among the most important deficiencies.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Effects of Weight”, p. 33

notes.front: How does overloading affect landing performance?
notes.back: A higher approach and landing speed, and a longer landing roll.
notes.explanation: Excessive weight reduces performance in almost every respect; these are among the most important deficiencies.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Effects of Weight”, p. 33

notes.front: Why does added weight reduce climb performance?
notes.back: The wing must meet the air at a steeper angle to hold height. That adds drag (air resistance), leaving less spare power for climbing.
notes.explanation: Designers work hard to minimise weight because of this marked effect.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Climb Performance Factors”, p. 22

notes.front: What happens to climb performance as altitude increases?
notes.back: It diminishes: more power is required while less is available.
notes.explanation: An increase in altitude increases the power required and decreases the power available. (Compare density altitude in topic 11.)
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Climb Performance Factors”, p. 22

notes.front: In steady level flight, how does lift compare with weight, and what happens if lift becomes less?
notes.back: Lift equals weight; if lift becomes less than weight, the aircraft starts to descend.
notes.explanation: Lift is the only force that counteracts weight.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Weight” and “Weight Control”, pp. 30 and 32

notes.front: What is the load factor in a level, coordinated turn at 60° of bank?
notes.back: 2 Gs.
notes.explanation: The wing must produce lift equal to twice the weight to hold altitude. Bank is how far the aircraft is tilted into the turn; a coordinated turn is one flown without slipping.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Load Factors in Steep Turns”, p. 31

notes.front: Beyond roughly what bank angle does load factor rise very rapidly?
notes.back: About 45° to 50°.
notes.explanation: It approaches, but never reaches, the 90° line, because a level 90° banked turn is not possible.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Load Factors in Steep Turns”, p. 31

notes.front: What are the two reasons load factors matter?
notes.back: A pilot can impose a dangerous overload on the structure, and a higher load factor raises the stalling speed.
notes.explanation: Stalls then become possible at seemingly safe speeds.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Load Factors”, p. 30

notes.front: How does an aircraft’s stalling speed change as load factor increases?
notes.back: It rises in proportion to the square root of the load factor.
notes.explanation: Doubling the stall speed therefore needs four times the load factor.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Load Factors and Stalling Speeds”, p. 31

notes.front: Figure: load factor chart. What load factor does the chart give for a 60° bank?
notes.explanation: Read across from 60° in the table, or up from 60° on the graph.
notes.source: FAA, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 2

notes.explanation: At shallow banks the load factor stays close to 1; it climbs steeply only past about 45°–50°.

notes.front: An aircraft stalls at 50 knots in level flight. At what speed can it stall under a load factor of 4?
notes.back: 100 knots: 50 knots × √4.
notes.explanation: Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Load Factors and Stalling Speeds”, p. 31

notes.front: A fixed-wing drone is flown in a tight 60° banked turn at low speed near the ground. What risks increase?
notes.back: Load factor doubles to 2 Gs, raising the stall speed; a stall so low leaves little room to recover.
notes.explanation: Sudden loss of control in steep turns near the ground has caused many accidents.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Load Factors and Stalling Speeds”, p. 32

notes.front: Are manufacturers’ performance data standardized?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Each manufacturer presents its data differently, so read your own aircraft’s figures carefully.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.1, p. B-1

notes.front: If the manufacturer publishes no performance data, what is advisable?
notes.back: Seek data already determined and published by other users of the same model, and use it as a starting point.
notes.explanation: Some reference is better than guessing the aircraft’s capabilities.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.1, p. B-1

notes.front: Your newly bought drone came with no performance figures. How should you plan its endurance and payload limits?
notes.back: Use performance data published by other users of the same model as a starting point.
notes.explanation: AC 107-2A advises using other users’ data as a starting point when the maker publishes none.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.1, p. B-1

notes.front: Your drone lifts its full payload easily at a sea-level site. Tomorrow you fly at a 7,000 ft site on a hot afternoon. What should you consider?
notes.back: Reducing weight: the high density altitude may leave it unable to perform safely at maximum weight.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: the maximum takeoff weight is the same everywhere
B) Reducing the payload weight
C) Adding ballast to stabilise it in thinner air
notes.choicesExplained: A: the limit is the same, but the aircraft may not safely lift it in high density altitude conditions. C: extra weight worsens performance further.
notes.explanation: High elevation and high temperature both raise density altitude and reduce takeoff and climb performance.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.2.1.1, p. B-1

notes.front: A drone releases a 2 lb package mounted under one arm. What should the remote PIC have worked out beforehand?
notes.back: How the CG will shift when the load is released, and whether it stays within limits.
notes.explanation: Expending a load changes both weight and balance; performance improves but balance may worsen.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.2.2, p. B-1

notes.front: After mounting a new sensor on one side, the drone keeps tilting towards that side and needs constant stick input to hold level. Which loading problem is most likely?
notes.back: The CG is outside its limits.
notes.explanation: Operating with the CG outside approved limits results in control difficulty; move or remove weight.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Weight and Balance”, p. 32

notes.front: A drone with an extra battery takes longer to climb, tops out lower and lands faster than usual. What is the likely cause?
notes.back: Overloading: excessive weight.
notes.explanation: Reduced climb, lower maximum altitude and higher landing speed are classic effects of excess weight.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Effects of Weight”, p. 33

notes.front: Before a flight with a new payload, what should the remote PIC verify about weight?
notes.back: That the total weight and its distribution are within the manufacturer’s weight and balance limits.
notes.explanation: AC 107-2A says to verify correct loading before any flight.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.2.1, p. B-1

notes.front: Stability versus controllability: what is the difference?
notes.back: Stability: the aircraft’s own tendency to return to its flight path. Controllability: how it responds to the pilot’s inputs.
notes.explanation: Controllability is the quality of the response to control, regardless of the aircraft’s stability characteristics.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Stability”, p. 30

notes.front: Excess weight versus CG out of limits: what does each mainly cause?
notes.back: Excess weight: poorer performance and structural risk. CG out of limits: control difficulty.
notes.explanation: Both can make flight unsafe, so check both before flight.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Weight and Balance”, p. 32

notes.front: Load factor versus weight: which changes during a turn?
notes.back: Weight stays the same; load factor rises, so the structure carries a multiple of that weight.
notes.explanation: At 60° of bank the structure carries twice the aircraft’s weight.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 4, “Load Factors in Steep Turns”, p. 31
